first.rationale: The two measurable declines are activation (-6%) and onboarding completion (-4%); the competitor's pricing move is real but responding to it with discounting is the option most likely to buy short-term acquisition at the cost of the stated objective, sustainable long-term qualified revenue (memory_73 records acquisition and revenue lift but says nothing about retention, margin, or cohort quality after the promo period). Onboarding is the direction where the observed metric decline, the mechanism, and the inherited evidence line up most directly, and its gains compound rather than decay. I spend the single verification pull on memory_86 because it is the most load-bearing claim for the action I intend and the one whose summary hides the most: 'lifting early product adoption' could mean completion-rate movement only, with no durable revenue or retention follow-through, and it may have been measured on a cohort mix unlike today's. memory_31 is a partial hedge on the same direction (SMB field-reduction, durable first-week lift), so if memory_86 fails verification the direction is not fully orphaned. Downstream value risk: shortening onboarding and cutting fields can strip the qualification signal that memory_44 says makes the enterprise sales-assisted path work, so the test should be scoped to self-serve SMB with the enterprise demo-request path untouched, and instrumented on downstream qualified revenue and 30/60-day retention rather than completion rate alone. All six memories are archived summaries of unknown vintage; the day-76 environment has shifted (new competitor pricing), so prior effect sizes are directional priors, not forecasts. Run with a holdout and a pre-committed kill condition rather than treating a completion-rate lift as success.

final.rationale: Verification came back clean and, importantly, richer than the summary: exp_86 showed completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. That last figure is the one that matters for the stated objective, because it means the completion lift was not purely cosmetic movement of accounts through a funnel; some of it persisted into retained usage. memory_31 independently points the same direction for SMB signup fields, so the direction now rests on two partially independent records rather than one. I commit the slot to simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale. Reasoning against the alternatives is unchanged: promotional_pricing (memory_73) is the intuitive answer to a competitor's entry pricing, but the record documents acquisition and revenue lift with no evidence on margin, cohort quality, or post-promo retention, which is precisely the trade the primary objective tells me not to make; and a price cut is hard to unwind once the market prices it in. activation_messaging (memory_91) targets the larger decline but is the weaker record, reporting week-one engagement and first meaningful action rather than any durable outcome. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: 30-day retention is not long-term qualified revenue, exp_86 ran in a pre-competitor environment, and the accounts most at risk right now are price-sensitive ones whose churn driver may be price rather than friction, so the prior effect size may not transfer. Downstream value risk stands: shortening onboarding can strip qualification signal that memory_44 says the enterprise demo-request path depends on, so scope this to self-serve SMB, leave the enterprise path untouched, and hold out a control. Instrument on downstream qualified revenue and 30/60-day retention, not completion rate, and pre-commit to killing it if completion rises while retention or qualified-revenue-per-cohort does not.
